analysis.one_liner: Lets private employers offer paid time off instead of cash overtime pay, at the worker's choice.
analysis.headline: One House Republican sponsored the bill and 12 more cosponsored it, but it never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires private employers to pay overtime in cash — time and a half for every extra hour. This bill would let employers offer workers a different deal: paid time off banked at one-and-a-half hours for every overtime hour, up to 160 hours, if the worker chooses it voluntarily before working the hours. Workers could demand cash for banked time in writing, unused time would be paid out every January 31 and again at termination at the higher of the rate when it was earned or the worker's final rate, and employers could not pressure workers over the choice. The whole program would end after five years unless Congress renews it.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who would rather have time than money — parents, caregivers, anyone who needs a block of days off more than a bigger paycheck — could bank overtime as paid time off at time-and-a-half, with guaranteed cash-out each year, at termination, or on written request. Employers that adopt a comp-time policy gain flexibility: they can offer time instead of cash, schedule when the time off is taken, and hold the overtime cost as a bank of hours until it is paid out or used.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who prefer time off; employers

how_it_helps.text: Private-sector workers could choose paid time off instead of cash overtime, earning 1.5 hours off for each overtime hour worked, up to a bank of 160 hours.

The choice must be made knowingly and voluntarily before the work is performed, not as a condition of employment, and employers are barred from intimidating, threatening, or coercing workers over the choice or from forcing them to use the time.

Banked time must be paid in cash at the higher of the rate when it was earned or the worker's final regular rate — every January 31 for unused time, upon termination, or within 30 days of a worker's written request.
The bill creates a private lawsuit remedy for workers: an employer that intimidates or coerces an employee over the choice owes the value of the banked hours plus an equal amount in damages.

For unionized workplaces, comp time can be offered only as the collective bargaining agreement allows, and the program would sunset after five years, with annual Government Accountability Office reports on usage, complaints, and enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who opt in give up the guaranteed cash premium in their next paycheck and can use the banked time only when the employer agrees it will not disrupt operations. Employers carry the payout liability and lawsuit risk for coercion, and the Labor Department takes on new notice and enforcement duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers who trade cash for banked time

drawbacks.text: The employer, not the worker, decides when banked time off can actually be taken: the bill requires time off be granted only if it does not 'unduly disrupt the operations of the employer.'
An employer that adopts a comp-time policy can discontinue it on 30 days' notice and cash out everyone's banked hours, so the arrangement lasts only as long as the employer wants it to.
Workers must have worked at least 1,000 hours for their employer in the previous 12 months to take part, which excludes many part-time and newer employees.

Protections against pressure are complaint-driven: the remedy for employer intimidation is a private lawsuit for the value of banked hours plus an equal amount in damages, which puts the burden on the worker to challenge coercion after the fact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives workers who would rather have time than money a real option, and this version is more protective than earlier comp-time proposals: annual cash-out, payout at termination at the higher rate, a written right to demand cash, a lawsuit remedy for coercion, and a five-year sunset. The weaknesses are structural, and an honest supporter should name them: only the employer can decide to offer comp time at all, only the employer can decide when banked time is actually used, and the worker's protection against pressure is a lawsuit after the fact rather than anything that stops the pressure. A worker living paycheck to paycheck can be steered toward time they may never get to take, while a worker with savings and a caregiving burden could genuinely benefit. It is a fair bargain for some workers and a risky one for the most economically vulnerable, and it is a clear flexibility and cash-flow gain for employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never came out — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Miller, an Illinois Republican, introduced the bill on March 17, 2021.
Its 12 cosponsors were all Republicans; no Democrat signed on.
The House sent it to the Education and Labor Committee the same day it was introduced, and that is the last action recorded for the bill.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: workers kept the existing guarantee of cash overtime, and employers gained none of the new scheduling flexibility. No group ended up with anything it did not already have — opponents of the change got their preferred outcome without anyone having to cast a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the overtime status quo held

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill sat without action in a committee controlled by Democrats, who never gave it a hearing.

industries.industry: Hourly-workforce employers (retail, food service, manufacturing, health care)
industries.note: Employers could offer time off in place of the overtime cash premium, holding that cost as a bank of hours until payout and scheduling the time off when it suits operations. Workers keep a voluntary choice with cash-out guarantees, so the employer's gain comes with real worker protections — but the employer also controls when the time off can actually be used.

In unionized workplaces, comp time can be provided only as the collective bargaining agreement allows, keeping unions as the required channel for any comp-time arrangement rather than shifting the choice to individual workers.
